Car Repair Costs: What to Know About Monthly Budgeting and Protection Plans

BY: Keith Benline
PUBLISHED September 04, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:12
Instaread

The average new vehicle costs just under $1,000 a month to own and operate based on the latest data released by AAA’s Your Driving Costs study. Serving as one of the more widely cited benchmarks for the true cost of car ownership, it’s an important number to consider when looking to purchase a vehicle.

That number covers fuel, insurance, financing, depreciation, and more, but it treats maintenance and repairs as a blended number. In practice, those two costs actually behave differently. Maintenance is something you can actually schedule and save for, but repairs will show up without warning. Typically, this happens in the least preferred month for your budget.

Building a monthly vehicle budget means separating those two items and deciding how to cover the unpredictable side, whether through a self-funded reserve, a vehicle protection plan, or some combination of both.

Predictable Costs vs. Unpredictable Costs

Routine maintenance, oil changes, tire rotations, brake pad replacement, filter swaps, and more all follow a set schedule based on mileage or time. You are capable of knowing roughly when it’s coming and what it will cost. This makes it quite easy to fold into your monthly budget. Endurance’s maintenance cost breakdown also provides a useful starting point for seeing typical costs by service type if you want to build in specific items.

Mechanical failure is the exact opposite. A transmission, an engine component, an electrical module, or a fuel system part can fail at any given moment and without warning. What’s worse is that the repair bill can run anywhere from a few hundred to several thousand dollars.

For example, per Kelley Blue Book (KBB), a transmission repair can cost anywhere from $2,900 to $7,100, depending on your make and model. Similarly, engine control module replacements can reach costs of $1,100 to $1,200 based on recent RepairPal data. Endurance offers a full sum average repair bill guide that you can also use to see samples of other amounts.

This unpredictability, both in timing and amount, is what actually throws a monthly budget off and exactly why putting protection in place is important.

What a Realistic Monthly Repair Reserve Looks Like

Should you want to set aside money for unpredictable repairs specifically, AAA recommends setting aside roughly $50 to $100 a month for a repair-and-maintenance fund, with older or higher-mileage vehicles needing more—some guidance puts that figure as high as $150 to $200 a month once a vehicle passes five years or 60,000 miles. This is because older, higher-mileage vehicles carry more failure risk. Endurance’s guide to average maintenance and repair cost breaks this down even further by vehicle age.

The math behind this is simple enough, but the problem isn’t math. It’s timing. A reserve in place only works if the first major failure waits until your fund has time to be built up. Most major failures, unfortunately, won’t wait for the calendar.

Where Most Owners Get Caught

As mentioned, if you’re planning to set aside money for a repair reserve, it can take time. For example, saving $150 a month will take you more than 19 months, over a year and a half, to cover just the low end of the transmission repair cost above. That’s assuming you start now, but most owners don’t get that runway.

A transmission or engine issue can show up well before that 1.5-year mark, and when it does, there are really only three options: use a credit card, drain savings meant for something else, or defer the repair and run major risks. None of those options is ideal, and all three are the direct result of unpredictable timing meeting a savings plan that needs time you don’t have.

How an Extended Warranty Converts Unpredictable Risk Into a Fixed Monthly Cost

An extended warranty, also referred to as a vehicle service contract (VSC) or auto protection plan, takes a different approach to the same issue. Instead of needing to save towards a repair that may or may not happen on schedule, you take care of a fixed monthly payment to have protection in place.

Qualified mechanical and electrical repairs will then be covered—minus your plan’s deductible—when they occur, regardless of whether your reserve has had time to build up. As an example, you can see the current Endurance Warranty coverage plans to compare what’s included at each level.

The comparison worth running is simple enough. If the monthly cost of a VSC is lower than what a self-insurance reserve would be based on your vehicle’s age, the coverage functions as a budgeting tool rather than an add-on. It’s not about trying to avoid repair costs, but rather about knowing the size of that line item every month instead of guessing it.

What an Extended Warranty Doesn’t Replace

An extended car warranty or service contract covers qualifying mechanical and electrical failures. It won’t cover the predictable routine maintenance, oil changes, brake pads, tires, and filters. Those remain your responsibility.

It’s worth noting, though, that taking care of those maintenance tasks is almost always required to keep a protection plan in good standing. It’s also one of the most effective ways to prevent the kinds of failures that would require the use of an emergency fund or activating the plan in the first place.

Putting a Monthly Ownership Budget Together

Putting together a complete monthly ownership budget for your vehicle should cover four main line items:

  1. Fuel: The ongoing cost of driving your vehicle around
  2. Car Insurance: Your liability and coverage premiums
  3. Maintenance Reserve: Any costs for scheduled upkeep on your vehicle, like oil changes, tires, brakes, and more
  4. Repair Coverage: The monthly cost associated with your self-funded reserve or a vehicle service contract

Seeing all of these line items together will give you a true picture of what your vehicle actually costs, rather than needing to discover each repair line item one at a time. A self-funded reserve can be a good option if your budget has room for it, but it takes time to develop and offers no coverage until it does.

An auto protection plan starts covering qualifying repairs from day one at a predictable monthly rate. For general repair cost information across common issues, Endurance’s repair resources are a useful starting point before deciding which approach fits your budget best.

Avoiding Costly Repair Bills Starts With Endurance

Car ownership costs are predictable until they aren’t. While you can schedule and budget for maintenance in advance, unexpected repairs are more challenging. That’s exactly the gap that a self-funded reserve struggles to close on its own.

Whether you build a dedicated repair fund, purchase a vehicle service contract, or use both together, the goal should always be the same. Turn an unpredictable expense into a number you can actually plan around.
